doc.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001

title: Jazz and freedom; mass in Russia and cancelled tours
summary: Brubeck argues dictators suppress jazz, which began as African-American freedom, and recalls the mass on Russian television and tours cancelled to protect audiences.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: A recent quote that you had about a CD of yours called “The Crossing,” you said it’s so important to have this message of freedom going all over the world, prophetic I think, even more important these days I think.

Oh absolutely. And well we’re confronted with that right now in this war in Afghanistan. And we are, to me, the country with by far the most freedom. And an example — why does everyone want to come here? And you know I’ve traveled so much and in almost every country in the world. And there are times when we’re hated you know. But they don’t ever seem to hate jazz. You know? Of course you’re getting a minority of people. But the idea of freedom, unless there’s — if there’s a dictator or a dictatorship, the first thing they’re going to stop is jazz. Absolutely. Hitler stopped it immediately. Stalin stopped it. I think it just gives the country, the people of a country, too much idea of what it would be like to be free. And you see that’s the way jazz started, was the African- American getting freedom, being denied freedom, and it still goes back to those roots of getting freedom. And people just don’t realize how little freedom there was. When you weren’t — some people weren’t allowed to speak but they would sing maybe or hum. Then, some way, they’ll get through. In Poland people that weren’t Catholic all started tipping their hats when they went by a Catholic church. Eventually this grew and grew, and of course they are mostly Catholic. But it just grew, where you couldn’t stop that. I

wrote a piece where it has a long section called “Bow Down” and it just goes over and over, bow down, to this great sacrament, all bow down. And one critic in England said, “how can you bow down to a sacrament?” Well you can. It was done and is still being done. Just this idea of that sacrament. And when we did the mass in Russia, and it was on Russian television maybe five years ago so all the old satellite countries saw it. Everybody in that choir had a crucifix. Where had they buried them? If you’d been caught with it you’re dead. Everybody in the audience followed this mass, just absolutely enthralled with it. And you see I’ve been through so many things where I’ve had to back off because freedom is so important that the people in the audience are going to be in trouble. And twice I had to cancel Russia because our ambassador said, “Dave, if you come the secret police are going to take everybody’s name at the door and they’ll lose all their privileges, and some of them are going to come anyway. They want to hear jazz and they want to hear you so badly.” But I canceled. Then when the Russians canceled the Olympics we canceled another tour. When the Russian plane was shot down with the Korean I think, remember that?
